definition: The advice taker was a hypothetical computer program, proposed by John McCarthy in his 1959 paper "Programs with Common Sense".
details: It was probably the first proposal to use logic to represent information in a computer and not just as the subject matter of another program. It may also have been the first paper to propose common sense reasoning ability as the key to Artificial Intelligence. In his paper, McCarthy advocated: "…programs to manipulate in a suitable formal language (most likely a part of the predicate calculus) common instrumental statements. The basic program will draw immediate conclusions from a list of premises. These conclusions will be either declarative or imperative sentences. When an imperative sentence is deduced the program takes a corresponding action." McCarthy justified his proposal as follows: "The main advantages we expect the advice taker to have is that its behaviour will be improvable merely by making statements to it, telling it about its symbolic environment and what is wanted from it. To make these statements will require little if any knowledge of the program or the previous knowledge of the advice taker. explainer.lead: The advice taker was John McCarthy's 1959 vision for a computer that could learn from plain instructions rather than reprogramming. It proposed that a machine with enough logical reasoning could absorb new knowledge like a person with common sense, making it one of the foundational ideas for how AI might actually think.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot that doesn't need new code every time you want it to do something new. Instead, you just tell it facts and goals in normal sentences, like "the kitchen is down the hall" and "bring me water," and it figures out the rest by itself. McCarthy wanted to build a machine that could reason from what it already knew plus what you just told it, the way a smart friend would.
tiers.practitioner: The advice taker remains unrealized as a complete system, but its principles directly inspired logic programming (Prolog), knowledge representation systems, and modern neuro-symbolic AI approaches. Engineers working in automated reasoning or expert systems still grapple with the same challenge: bridging formal logical inference with practical, scalable knowledge updates. The core pitfall is the brittleness of pure logical deduction—real environments require handling uncertainty, inconsistency, and incomplete information that predicate calculus alone cannot manage.
tiers.paperLevel: McCarthy (1959) proposed a program operating in a fragment of predicate calculus that would derive both declarative and imperative conclusions from premises, executing actions when imperative sentences were deduced. The formal requirement was that the program automatically deduce 'a sufficiently wide class of immediate consequences of anything it is told and what it already knows,' a property McCarthy identified with common sense. Known limits include the frame problem (specifying what does not change), the computational intractability of unrestricted logical consequence, and the difficulty of representing default reasoning or probabilistic knowledge within pure deductive frameworks.

explainer.example: You tell the advice taker: 'The conference room is east of the lab. My meeting is in the conference room. If my meeting is in a room, go to that room.' The program parses these into logical premises, deduces the imperative 'Go to the conference room,' and executes the action. Later you add 'The lab is closed for maintenance' and 'The backup room is west of the lobby,' plus 'If the lab is closed, use the backup room.' The advice taker recomputes, now deducing 'Go to the backup room' without any code changes.

usedIn.name: Logic programming (Prolog)
usedIn.detail: Direct descendant: programs that deduce conclusions from facts and rules stated declaratively

usedIn.name: Expert systems
usedIn.detail: Rule-based inference engines that derive actions from knowledge bases, though with narrower domains than McCarthy's vision

usedIn.name: Neuro-symbolic AI
usedIn.detail: Modern attempts to combine neural learning with explicit logical reasoning for more flexible knowledge manipulation

explainer.intuition: A computer that gets smarter simply by being told things, without anyone rewriting its code.
howItWorks: A human provides statements in a formal logical language, likely a subset of predicate calculus.
The program maintains a knowledge base of premises: facts about the world and goals.
An inference engine draws immediate logical conclusions from these premises.
If a conclusion is declarative, it is added to what the program knows; if imperative, the program executes the corresponding action.
New advice integrates with existing knowledge automatically, so behavior improves without reprogramming.
explainer.whyItMatters: The advice taker established the research agenda of knowledge representation and common-sense reasoning as central to AI, shifting focus from specialized problem-solving to general, teachable intelligence.
misconceptions: That it was ever built—it remained a proposal, not an implemented system.
That 'common sense' here means everyday intuition; McCarthy defined it technically as automatic deduction of immediate logical consequences.
That logical representation alone suffices for real-world AI; the proposal predated recognition of uncertainty, learning from data, and the frame problem.
